Le travail des inspecteurs de la STM sou: The work of STM inspectors under scrutiny
La femme noire reçoit des coups au visag: The Black woman is struck in the face by one of the officers.
Samedi dernier, une jeune femme prend le: Last Saturday, a young woman takes the metro. In a video that has made the rounds on social media, she can be seen being held down on the ground by inspectors from the Société de transport de Montréal (STM). The Black woman is struck in the face by one of the officers. Bystanders can also be seen trying to intervene.
La jeune femme appréhendée aurait reçu d: The young woman who was apprehended reportedly suffered head injuries that later required her to be hospitalized. The matter is under investigation, and the woman involved does not wish to speak to the media for now. The day after the incident, the STM presented its version of events in a press release. According to the STM, the passenger had not paid her fare and then refused to identify herself and cooperate. This is not the first time a video of this kind has made headlines.
En 2019, une scène filmée dans le métro: In 2019, a scene filmed in the Montréal metro showed STM inspectors beating 21-year-old Lawrence Juliano Gray with a baton. Several other cases of violence involving STM officers have been reported in the media and on social media in recent years.
Pour plusieurs, l’intervention de la sem: For many, last week’s intervention shows that it is time to question the use of force in interventions by STM officers.
Raph K. Yoyo witnessed the incident. Hearing piercing screams, he ran over and came upon the scene, which he filmed. “Two STM officers are pinning a Black woman to the ground. What struck me, like many internet users, is that at one point, the STM officer loses patience and repeatedly hits the victim on the ground, punching her in the face,” he says. “At least there were some brave people who stepped in.”
Il est le dernier à quitter les lieux ap: He was the last to leave the scene, after checking on the young woman’s condition. Mario Berniqué, a specialist in private and public security intervention and operations, knows the environment in which STM inspectors work well. “Often, with the STM, or with security guards, it starts with a minor offence,” he explains. “A person refuses to identify themselves or to cooperate, there’s an escalation, and it becomes a summary offence under the Code of Penal Procedure. It goes all the way to arrests and the use of force,” he laments.
Selon M. Yoyo, rien ne peut justifier qu: According to Mr. Yoyo, nothing can justify an officer in a position of authority acting this way.
« L’inspecteur qui a perdu son sang-froi: “The inspector who lost his cool was clearly not following a process that would defuse the situation or prevent an escalation of violence,” he continues.
« Les inspecteurs sont formés pour suivr: “Inspectors are trained to follow the use-of-force model taught at the École nationale de police du Québec (ENPQ), which is based in particular on the principle that the force used must be proportional to the degree of resistance and aggression of the person being apprehended,” the STM explains to La Converse. Security officers receive mandatory 14-week training at the Nicolet police school. Mr. Berniqué has trained STM officers and police forces. “The use of force is the last resort,” he says. According to him, the means officers use depend on the context, the situation and many other factors, and there are rules to follow. “It’s not an organized fight; it’s a manoeuvre to enforce a law,” sums up the retired police officer.
Ce n’est pas ce qu’a vu M. Yoyo à la sta: That is not what Mr. Yoyo saw at Jean-Talon station. “When you put force in the hands of individuals, you have to make sure they follow a clear protocol,” he believes. “Don’t kill me, you can’t kill me”—that is what, according to Ralph Yoyo, the woman being apprehended was screaming. On site, he learned that the alleged offender had just immigrated to the country. “We don’t know her situation, where she’s from. She’s scared, and before losing his cool, the officer yells at her to put her hands behind her back,” says Mr. Yoyo, who believes the inspector made the situation worse.
« ll est totalement à côté de la situati: “He is completely out of touch with the situation he’s reacting to. Does he understand the person in front of him?” he asks. “If officers don’t have adequate training, why are they allowed to intervene?”
Mario Berniqué suggère que les façons de: Mario Berniqué suggests that the way things are done could be reviewed. “All technical manoeuvres can be carried out if society accepts them. If they aren’t tolerated, training has to be adapted to social rules and political orientations,” he sighs in an interview. Drawing on his long experience, he adds that it is blunders and accidents that lead to training being adjusted.
La STM a déclaré que la force utilisée é: The STM stated that the force used during the April 17 incident was reasonable. Alexandre Norris, of the Commission de la sécurité publique de Montréal, called on April 19 for an independent investigation to shed light on the matter. A few days later, the STM announced that an internal investigation would take place.
« Lorsqu’une entité enquête sur elle-mêm: “When an entity investigates itself, questions are immediately raised about the credibility of such an investigation, and rightly so,” the commission’s chair points out in an interview. “We want credible, independent investigations of such events,” Norris specifies.
La société de transport montréalaise a e: The Montréal transit authority then corrected course by calling on an independent expert in ethics to investigate the incident. The expert in question, lawyer Marco Gaggino, previously represented the Association des policiers provinciaux du Québec (APPQ) before the Viens Commission in 2017.
Il a également représenté Mathieu Chambe: He also represented Mathieu Chamberland, a police officer brought before the ethics committee and accused of use of force without legal justification, abuse of authority and intimidation against an alleged 16-year-old victim. The STM declined to comment further on the matter.
Alain Babineau, consultant en matière de: Alain Babineau, a security and racial profiling consultant, examines the role of STM inspectors. “We have to keep in mind that they are not police officers. They are security officers who ensure safety and proper functioning,” he explains. In his view, their job must be clear so that their conduct is clear as well. “Is it worth provoking a physical altercation at that level?
Au bout de la ligne, c’est la sécurité d: At the end of the day, what matters is the safety of passengers and users, well beyond collecting $3.50,” he points out. The former police officer believes that peace officers and security officers who deal with all kinds of people must show humanity. “You have to have compassion and focus on the human side,” Mr. Babineau believes. “You have to look at the circumstances, the situation of the person you’re stopping—see, for example, whether they’re vulnerable, whether they have mental health issues, whether they’re in a precarious financial situation. “You have to have compassion.”
Si la situation se répète, il suggère un: If the situation recurs, he suggests a psychosocial intervention.
M. Babineau affirme sans détour que la S: Mr. Babineau states bluntly that the STM is not free of racial profiling, like all law enforcement or security organizations. “Racial profiling is also found in the use of excessive force,” he says.
À la suite d’une demande déposée il y a: Following a request submitted a year ago to the ministère de la Sécurité publique, inspectors in the STM’s Security and Control division will obtain special constable status starting in July. This news is worrying to many, who are concerned about the additional powers that will be granted to these officers. These powers give them the right to make arrests without having witnessed an offence and to access police databases. They also give them the possibility of carrying weapons.
Pour assurer cette transition, qui se fe: To ensure this transition, which will be gradual, the STM’s 160 inspectors will undergo additional training at the École nationale de police du Québec. Marvin Rotrand, a former STM vice-chair and Snowdon city councillor, says the new powers of special constables are a step toward the militarization of public transit. The STM has said it will not authorize its inspectors to carry weapons, but it has not specified what it means by “weapons.”
M. Rotrand estime qu’en dépit des demand: Mr. Rotrand believes that, despite public demands, doubt remains on this issue. “Whether or not it’s the STM’s intention, once inspectors become special constables, it’s the Société’s decision. Constables could be armed far more than the STM lets on,” he fears. Rémi Boivin, an associate professor of criminology at UQAM and chair of the Committee on Relations between STM Inspectors and the Community (CRIC), worked with the STM as an external expert to help with the transition of the Société’s inspectors.
Joint au téléphone, il explique que plus: Reached by phone, he explains that several members of the committee he chairs have expressed concerns, particularly about racial profiling, but also said they were hopeful that the changes would be for the better. “It’s not only about having more powers, but about seeing the job through,” he sums up.
Les inspecteurs qui patrouillent le rése: The inspectors who patrol the network currently act as public servants. The STM reminds us that they are subject to the STM Code of Ethics. Their new status as special constables will subject them to the Police Act and to the authority of the Police Ethics Commissioner. The Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI) may also be called upon to investigate.
M.Babineau se réjouit du fait que les en: Mr. Babineau is pleased that investigations can now be carried out by experts in the field and considers that this measure will make special constables much more accountable. “They’re going to have to be careful, because instead of reporting internally, they’ll be reporting to the Police Ethics Commissioner’s office. The bar is much higher when it comes to evaluating conduct,” he argues. Marvin Rotrand also says the inspectors’ new status will complicate the way complaints filed against them are handled.
« La procédure peut prendre des années »: “The process can take years,” he says of ethics proceedings. “Nobody wants a complaint to determine whether officers used excessive force to take several years, but that’s what’s likely to happen,” he lets slip. In a report, Rémi Boivin made several recommendations, including consultations aimed at helping the public understand the need for a legal designation and an external accountability structure.
« L’intervention du week-end dernier est: “Last weekend’s intervention is a very good example of why inspectors should be special constables,” he believes, explaining that the inspectors’ new status requires that incidents be investigated by an external entity and that the findings be made public.
Dans le but d’améliorer ses services, la: In an effort to improve its services, the STM rolled out a new “proximity strategy” on March 25. It aims to bring inspectors closer to the communities present in their workplace, <l1>an approach that is gaining ground in policing</l1>. “Concretely, two service regions will be created to foster a socio-community approach and the building of ties between inspectors and the clientele in the area,” reads the transit authority’s website.
Theodros Wolde, président du chapitre de: Theodros Wolde, president of the LaSalle chapter of the community organization ACORN Canada, condemned the force used by STM officers during last week’s incident. He does not see that any such rapprochement is taking place. He laments that violent incidents have been multiplying for some time and that they disproportionately affect vulnerable people. “These could be people who don’t know how public transit works, or who are poor,” he suggests. The community worker, who is also an accountant, says that people living in poverty are racialized or immigrants. “It’s a systemic problem,” he says of the stops and the use of force.
C’est l’usage excessif de la force qui a: It was excessive use of force that convicted Derek Chauvin, the police officer who killed George Floyd. Here too, excessive use of force kills and injures and, most often, harms vulnerable and racialized people. “In our society, police services are the only institution, besides the military, that can use deadly force,” says security and racial profiling consultant Alain Babineau. “Convincing 12 jurors and proving every element of the charges beyond a reasonable doubt is not an easy thing, especially since you’re starting with a police officer who, de facto, has the power to use force.” The former police officer also believes that officers must speak up if they witness problematic behaviour by their colleagues.
